units: one of the two cloths comes from the fleece clipped off a farmed animal
the other cloth is drawn from a plant after soaking and crushing
the curled animal fibers hold warmth by trapping air
the plant cloth yields a smooth yarn that feels cool to the touch

text: Lay two cloths side by side on a workbench and they will tell opposite stories. One begins as a fleece clipped off a herd animal, and its crimped fibers trap pockets of air, which is how they hold on to warmth. The other starts as a plant stalk soaked until it softens, then crushed and combed into a smooth yarn that feels cool under the fingers. A weaver builds on that split. Animal fiber goes into cold-weather clothing, where a thick weave slows the heat as it escapes. Plant fiber goes into shirts, because it carries damp away from the skin. Washing tells the two apart all over again. Hot water makes the animal fiber shrink and mat together, while the plant cloth takes wash after wash and simply creases at every fold. Choosing a cloth means choosing a climate, and choosing how you will look after it.

units: the narrator visits the workroom of a neighbor who sews

text: The woman who lives next door sews, and one rainy evening she opened her workroom to me. Until then I had understood nothing at all about the clothes I put on every morning. She started with her cloth, which she keeps stacked by kind: soft cottons, coarse weaves that scratch the palm, fine knits that unravel the moment a pin catches them. Then came the tools, a battered thimble, a pair of scissors that nobody else may touch, a flat stick of chalk for marking. After that she showed me her hands at work, and there I lost the thread completely. She builds a cuff, drops a lining into a jacket, and never stops to measure twice. Last of all she talked about her customers, the ones who come back with cheap jackets that gape at the shoulder. She laughs about it, picks up her needle, and saves the thing.

units: the first step is to put the trousers on in front of a mirror

specialists advise a fitting before the pins come out
text: Shortening a pair of trousers at home demands a method, and every alterations workshop prescribes the same succession of operations, always in that order. Put the trousers on in front of a mirror, fold the cloth up to the height you want, and mark that line with a row of pins placed close together. Take them off, open the old edge with a seam ripper, then press the fold flat so that the earlier crease disappears for good. Now cut, and leave a margin of cloth below the marked line, or the whole job can never be undone. Turn the extra under, pin it down, and fasten it with stitching that stays off the outer face. A last pass with the iron settles the edge. The professionals who do this for a living always repeat the same warning: try the trousers on once more before a single pin comes out.

units: an idle textile mill set in a valley has started working again

text: The mill had stood silent at the bottom of the valley, and now its looms have started beating again. The cause is a quiet turn in taste, nothing grander than that. Buyers grew tired of knits that pill after a wash or two, and they began asking for longer, tighter, costlier yarn. That demand put a price back on the fleeces raised nearby, which farmers used to burn for want of anyone willing to take them. From there the effect spread outward. Carding sheds reopened, a dye house lit its vats again, and workrooms relearned how to set a neckline by hand. The technical manager puts it plainly: the weave of a sweater tells you how a whole region is faring. One shadow hangs over all of it. Trained hands are scarce, and learning the trade asks for a patience few applicants will give.

units: the work garment described takes more strain than office clothing

text: A builder's jacket takes strain that office clothing never has to meet. At the shoulder, the armhole opens and closes from dawn until dusk, and the seam there gives way long before anything else does. At the pockets, the weight of tools drags the cloth downward and pulls the front of the jacket out of shape. At the elbows, rubbing against rough surfaces wears the weave right through to a hole. Manufacturers answer each fault on its own terms. They widen the armhole and set a triangular gusset under the arm to take up the movement. They back every pocket and lock its corners with extra stitching. They lay a patch of heavy cloth over the elbow, and it can be swapped out without taking the whole sleeve apart. The lining stays removable, so it comes out once the cold season ends.

units: the text sets two wardrobes against each other

text: Set two wardrobes against each other and examine them closely. The first holds a handful of garments, each one chosen slowly, and several have lasted past their tenth year and carry mending that anyone can see. The second is crammed with things bought on impulse, worn for a single season, then dropped because the knit went slack or a buttonhole tore at the first snag. People reach for the family budget as the explanation. It does not hold, since the owner of the crowded wardrobe spent more. What divides the two habits is the attention paid to how a garment was made. Look at a seam, tug a loose thread, turn back a collar to judge the lining. Such verifications cost nothing and weed out the articles that are already doomed. We ought to teach them the way we teach reading a food label.

text: The mender works in a narrow room at the back of a shopping arcade, and her trade falls into three distinct branches. First come the accidents, a tear at the knee, a buttonhole stretched out of shape, an edge ripped open by the heel of a shoe. Then comes fitting the body in front of her, which consumes the greater part of her week, since a factory size corresponds to almost nobody's real silhouette. She takes in a back, tightens a slack neckline, shortens a sleeve by a whisker. Last comes remaking, the part of the work she likes best. A dress nobody wears becomes a skirt, and a worn coat gives up its lining to another. She learned all of it from an older tailor, then spent two decades sharpening the craft entirely on her own. She turns away any apprentice who arrives in a hurry.

units: the narrator judges his coat badly during the first cold season

text: Honestly, this coat had me doubting it for quite a while at the beginning. That first winter the collar kept flipping up, the gathers across the back puffed out in an odd way, and the color looked drab beside my previous jacket. By the second winter the cloth had softened and taken the shape of my shoulders, and the lapels finally hung straight on their own. The third winter was the best of them. It rained without any letup whatsoever, the surface drank the water and dried overnight, and nothing ever smelled off. Then the lining split under one arm and I thought the coat was finished. A mender charged me a tenth of what I had paid for it, and off it went for another round of service. I would tell anyone to buy one, as long as you can live with it looking ugly the first year.

text: Dear sister, I am writing before the crate leaves, because what is inside it needs a proper word of explanation. You will be getting our father's blue jacket. I am not sending it along out of sentiment. Damp under the roof had begun eating away at the lining, and a garment left in a trunk ends up chewed through by moths. The outer cloth has held, and that is exactly why I decided it was worth saving. You will find the right cuff frayed. That comes from years of an arm resting on a workbench, which polished the weave away in that particular spot. A seamstress promised me that a piece taken from under the collar would make the repair invisible. Have it done, then wear it without the slightest worry. Cloth of that kind stiffens while it hangs and loosens once you put it on.

units: the text deals with the insect that damages woolen knits

text: Should we fear the insect that riddles our woolens? The question comes back at the close of every cold season, when the knitted things go into storage. It is not the winged adult that eats the yarn but its larva, blind and tiny, drawn toward animal fibers and above all toward the traces of sweat soaked into them. Hence the first answer: a garment washed clean feeds that larva poorly. And the storing itself? A closed, opaque bag beats an open shelf, and two nights in the cold will kill the eggs laid along a seam. What about the scented sachets our grandmothers tucked between the piles? They drive the pest off without killing it, and the effect fades fast. The lasting cure is a thoroughly dull habit. Pull the woolens out, shake them, air them, and fold them a different way.
